the development of nanoporous and nanosized structures for enhanced bioactivity.

the fabrication and characterization of nanoporous and nanocolumnar structures of tantalum oxide (Ta2O), niobium oxide (Nb2O), zirconia oxide (ZrO) and titanium oxide (TiO) via electrochemical anodization.
the fabrication of nanoporous and nanoscale titania and zirconia via anodization and their bioactivities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the nanoporous tantalum oxide (Ta2O3) is the most promising material for future biomedical applications.
the nanoporous tantalum oxide exhibited the most promising bioactivity and the nanoporous niobium oxide demonstrated the most promising biofunctionality.
the nanoporous structure of Ta2O 5 exhibited the best bioactivity, while the nanotubular structure of ZrO2 showed the worst.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tantalum oxide is the most promising candidate for biomedical applications, and the bioactivity of niobium oxide, zirconium oxide and titania can be enhanced by annealing.

the nanoporous tantalum oxide exhibited the most superior biocompatibility and bioactivity, while the nanoporous niobia and nanotublar titania exhibited the lowest bioactivity, among the four kinds metal oxide nanotubular structures.
the bioactivity of metal oxide nanostructures could be enhanced via the surface energy, which is closely related to the surface morphology and roughness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nanoporous and the nanotubular structures of Ta2O, Nb2O, ZrO, and TiO have the potential to improve the bioactivity of tantalum and niobium implants.
the nanoporous and tubular layers of Ta, Nb, Zr, and Ti are promising materials for enhanced bioactivity, and can be used to improve the biocompatibility of other metal implants.
nanoporous and nanofibrous Ta2O5 and Nb2O5 are the most promising candidates for biomedical application, especially for dental implants.
